parsed.explanation: The combined operative regime pairs a broadly protective subnational jurisdiction with an actively hostile national layer the visitor cannot avoid. Within the state/province, protections are documented as operating: public-accommodation and hate-crime protections covering gender identity, self-ID markers including X, no facility ban, an explicit care-shield law, and identity-based prison placement. But every entry into the country passes the national regime: binary sex passports, refusal instructions for perceived document discrepancy, potential permanent fraud findings, X markers blocked or confiscated, detentions of foreign trans citizens reported by allied governments, and federal facility/custody rules if the traveller crosses into federal custody. Those are universal-exposure, tier-1/near-tier-1 national exposures with no remedy this state can override; the state's protections mitigate only the local journey. Result: materially above the parent regime's national average, but capped below protective-jurisdiction levels by the border/document exposure.

entry_documents.exposure: National passport regime forces binary sex markers; travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, some stranded abroad. Visa cable directs officers to refuse cases with document discrepancy and consider permanent fraud ineligibility. Eight foreign governments issued trans-specific travel advisories after detentions.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; litigation ongoing; legal-aid FAQ exists. State X markers and licences remain locally valid.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry screening is wholly national; the state's protective document regime cannot displace federal passport/visa adjudication.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National custody: conversion-therapy-style policies for trans inmates, hormone denial, forced labour, beatings, sexual abuse in immigration custody; reporting discontinued. Entry friction can cascade into detention.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: State corrections house trans women by gender identity, documented in practice; state hate-crime statute with enhancements.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A visa problem or federal investigation places the traveller under national custody rules, not state placement practice.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans access to federally funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity; 9+ state/provinces impose birth-sex facility bans, 4 with criminal exposure; airport screening flagged as outing risk nationally.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This state/province has no facility restriction; its highest court affirmed identity-aligned school facilities; TSA-style screening is national.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: Federal buildings, transport hubs and national facilities follow the national rule even inside the protective state.

care_services.exposure: National orders frame trans care as mutilation; insurance reimbursement rules threatened; hospital records subpoenaed nationally; visitors may face care barriers outside the state.
care_services.protection: State law explicitly protects gender-affirming healthcare (2024); minors 16+ may access hormone therapy; identity-inclusive health data mandated.
care_services.interaction: State shield governs care sought within the state; national funding and insurance mechanisms remain federal overrides.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National orders and counterterrorism strategy frame gender ideology and 'radically pro-transgender' groups as security threats; enforcement directives target schools and facilities; 2026 legislative season documented as degrading rights.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State statutes prohibit gender-identity discrimination and hate crimes; panic defence abolished; state placed in low-risk group by national assessment.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: State police and courts operate protectively, but federal investigative and prosecutorial authority cannot be displaced by the state.

minors_guardians.exposure: National orders criminalise facilitation of trans minors' social transition, subpoena minors' hospital records, and ban care in 27 state/provinces; travelling families face federal document rules; national sports restrictions applied by the state university system.
minors_guardians.protection: State care shield, marker rules for minors (with parental consent), no local facility ban.
minors_guardians.interaction: A minor accompanied by a guardian is locally protected but crosses the same federal entry regime; sports compliance shows national pressure penetrating state institutions.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No state-specific violence figures in the inventory; national hostility climate is documented. Not established at state level.
street_violence_police_response.protection: State hate-crime enhancement and anti-discrimination enforcement are documented protections.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State response to incidents is protective; national climate raises baseline exposure.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: Passport litigation unresolved; whether university sports compliance persists is unknown; no state violence statistics; sanctuary bill stalled after public backlash.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Surviving repeal referenda show durable state protections; running legal-aid documentation support exists.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Changing federal court outcomes can shift the operative national regime mid-travel; state protections are stable.

anchor_checks.comparison: This state has none of that anchor's universal local facility exclusion or adverse court findings — locally it is far safer. But it sits inside a parent regime whose passport/visa screening, facility orders and custody practices resemble 0.35-A's tier-1 exposure at the national level, which the state cannot displace at entry.

0.55-B shows local hostility partially remedied under a neutral parent. Here the direction is reversed: strong local protections under a hostile parent. The exposures are at the border, not the guesthouse, and are more severe (stranding, fraud bars, detention), but less frequent within the visit itself.

0.75-C pairs acceptance with only a dead-letter tangential statute. This jurisdiction's negative layer is active and enforced (passport refusals, custody abuse, advisories), not dead paper, so it sits well below. Its local protections are comparable in strength to 0.75-C's documented service remedies.

parsed.synthesis: The traveller encounters two interacting regimes. Locally, documented protections actually operate: identity-based markers, care shields, anti-discrimination law, identity-aligned custody, no facility ban — placing the in-state journey near the 0.75–0.85 tier. Nationally, the entry and document regime is a current, universal, unremedied exposure: binary marker enforcement, documented passport confiscation and stranding, refusal-and-fraud instructions, custody abuse, and foreign-government advisories confirming real detentions. Because entry precedes every visit and follows the traveller into federal facilities and any custody encounter, the hostile national layer caps the score; the protective state layer raises it well above the parent's own average. Net: ~0.65 — reduced risk inside the state, materially elevated at the border and in any federal-custody cascade, with the minor-facing national measures an added, unresolved exposure.
